nameStory: The Golden Eagle gets its name from the beautiful golden-brown feathers that shine like burnished metal on the back of its head and neck. This gleaming 'golden crown' catches sunlight as the bird soars, creating a distinctive shimmer that sets it apart from other dark-colored eagles. The scientific name Aquila comes from the Latin word for eagle, while chrysaetos means 'golden eagle' in Greek.
description: The Golden Eagle is one of North America's most magnificent birds of prey, soaring on wings that can span over 7 feet across. These powerful hunters are primarily dark chocolate brown all over, with that distinctive golden-bronze plumage shining on their head and neck. Young Golden Eagles look quite different, sporting white patches on their wings and a white band across their tail that they lose as they mature into adults. They're built for hunting with incredibly strong talons and sharp, hooked beaks perfect for catching rabbits, ground squirrels, and other prey.

idTips.label: Golden head plumage
idTips.description: The back of the head and neck gleam with golden-bronze feathers that catch sunlight like polished metal, contrasting beautifully with the dark brown body

idTips.label: Wing shape in flight
idTips.description: Wings held in a slight 'V' shape when soaring, with long 'fingers' of feathers spread at the wingtips that you can count against the sky

idTips.label: Size and build
idTips.description: Massive birds with 6-7 foot wingspans that dwarf hawks and even most other eagles, with a powerful, stocky build and broad chest

idTips.label: Juvenile white markings
idTips.description: Young birds show crisp white patches on their wings and a bright white band across the base of their tail, visible even from great distances

idTips.label: Flight style
idTips.description: Soars effortlessly for long periods with minimal wing flapping, riding thermals and updrafts with incredible grace and stability

habitat: Golden Eagles prefer remote, mountainous areas and large stretches of open country in northern New England, particularly in New Hampshire's White Mountains and northern Vermont. They hunt over alpine meadows, rocky ridges, and expansive forests, often soaring along mountain ridgelines where updrafts help them cover vast territories. Look for them near cliffs and rocky outcrops where they build their massive stick nests, usually far from human development.

seasonality.spring: Breeding pairs return to their cliff-top nests, adding fresh sticks and lining materials. This is when you're most likely to see courtship flights with dramatic aerial displays over their territory.
seasonality.summer: Adults are busy hunting to feed their young, making regular flights between nest sites and hunting grounds. Young eagles may be visible in nests on cliff faces through binoculars.
seasonality.fall: Newly independent juvenile eagles disperse widely, making this the best time to spot them as they wander through New England. Migration brings additional birds through the region.
seasonality.winter: Some individuals remain year-round in suitable habitat, while others move to lower elevations. They may be seen soaring on warm winter days when thermals develop.

funFact: A Golden Eagle's nest can weigh as much as a small car! These massive structures, called eyries, are built on cliff ledges and added to year after year, sometimes reaching 10 feet deep and weighing over 2,000 pounds - some have been used continuously by generations of eagles for over 100 years.
confusionNotes: Golden Eagles are most often confused with Turkey Vultures when soaring, but remember 'Golden eagles are golden, vultures are wobbly' - Turkey Vultures rock unsteadily side-to-side in flight and hold their wings in a much more pronounced V-shape, while Golden Eagles soar steadily with wings nearly flat.
contextualKnowledge: Golden Eagles have been revered by many Indigenous cultures as symbols of power and spiritual connection, and they remain the national bird of several countries including Mexico and Germany. In New England, they were nearly eliminated by DDT and habitat loss but are slowly recovering, though they remain uncommon with only about 80 observations recorded in the region.
compareHints: Golden Eagles are the only members of the 'true eagle' genus Aquila in New England, making them unique among local raptors. Compared to our more common Bald Eagles, Golden Eagles are slightly smaller, completely feathered legs (Bald Eagles have bare yellow legs), and lack the white head and tail of adult Bald Eagles. Golden Eagles also prefer mountainous terrain while Bald Eagles stick closer to water bodies.
